title: Diwali: from darkness to light
hookLine: Krishna opens a demon king's prison, and the lamps go on before dawn
carry: from darkness, lead me to light
last: DURGA: THE POWER OF EVERY GOD, AS MOTHER.

lines: FIVE A.M., WARM OIL, A BATH.
IN THE NORTH, LAMPS FOR RAMA.
A KING WHO LOCKED PEOPLE IN THE DARK.
cards: Five in the morning, still pitch dark, in a house in south India. A grandmother is rubbing warm oil into a sleepy child's hair before a bath.
Firecrackers are already popping down the street, and a pattern of colored powder waits at the door. Far to the north, people are waiting for tonight's lamps for Rama, the story you already know.
Here, the lamps go on before sunrise, for a different story: Krishna, and a demon king who kept thousands of people locked in the dark.

teach.b: The Bhagavata Purana tells it. A demon king named Narakasura has grown so strong that he's stolen the earrings of Aditi, the mother of the gods, and locked away more than sixteen thousand princesses in his fortress.

teach.h: KRISHNA AND SATYABHAMA OPEN THE PRISON.
teach.b: Krishna flies there on Garuda, the great eagle, with his queen Satyabhama beside him. He breaks through walls of fire and water, defeats Naraka's five-headed guard, Mura, and then Naraka himself.
In many southern tellings, it's Satyabhama who strikes the final blow. Then the prison is thrown open, and sixteen thousand women walk out into the light.
A popular telling adds that Naraka, dying, asked to be remembered with lamps.
So on Naraka Chaturdashi, many families wake before dawn, bathe with oil, and light lamps while it's still dark. In the north, the lamps are for Rama coming home.
On the main night, the new moon, many families welcome Lakshmi, the goddess of fortune and well-being, with open doors. Jains and Sikhs light lamps in this season too, for their own stories.
Now the teaching under all of them.

teach.h: FROM DARKNESS, LEAD ME TO LIGHT.
teach.b: An old prayer from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, still chanted today, asks: lead me from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to what doesn't die.
The Upanishad itself explains it: the darkness is death; the light is what doesn't die. Many teachers also hear it as a prayer to wake from not-knowing into what's real.
Every Diwali lamp is that prayer, made of clay and oil. It's why a family lights clay lamps in a house full of electric light. The lamp isn't for seeing the room.
It's asking to see what's real.

how: For Diwali, Hindu families clean and decorate their homes, draw rangoli patterns at the door, light rows of clay lamps, worship Lakshmi on the new-moon night, share sweets, and visit relatives; customs and the stories told vary by region over the festival's five days.

o: a night of fasting and silent prayer
a row of lamps on the darkest night
a harvest feast under the full moon

s: everyone lights the Diwali lamps for the same story
Rama's return in much of the north, Krishna and Narakasura in much of the south, Lakshmi for many.
the Diwali lamps carry an old Upanishad prayer: from darkness, lead me to light
tamaso ma jyotir gamaya, from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, still chanted today.
in the Bhagavata, Krishna defeats Narakasura and frees his captives
the prison is thrown open and the women walk out into the light.

games.q: it's 5 a.m. on Diwali, pitch dark. your nani is lighting a lamp before the sun is even up. what is the lamp saying?
o: the power's out, so we need light.
from darkness, lead me to light.
it's a signal for the fireworks to start.
games.why: every Diwali lamp carries the old prayer, tamaso ma jyotir gamaya. lit in the dark, for a prison opened and a king come home.

practice: Light one light if you can: a diya, a candle, even a phone screen turned toward you. If you pray, say the old line slowly, three times: tamaso ma jyotir gamaya, from darkness lead me to light.
Then think of one place in your life where you can't see yet: a decision, a worry, a question about who you really are. Don't fix it. Just hold the light up to it, and ask to see.
If you don't pray, simply ask the question, and sit with the flame.

wordCard.voice: Diwali. The row of lamps: many stories, one prayer, lit on the darkest night of the month.

orig.note: Sanskrit, from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad: 'from darkness, lead me to light.'

carryVoice: Your line: from darkness, lead me to light. Every lamp says it. Day eighty-one, done.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.3.28 (asato ma sad gamaya, tamaso ma jyotir gamaya, mrtyor ma amrtam gamaya, with the text's own gloss)
Bhagavata Purana 10.59 (Krishna, Satyabhama and Narakasura; Mura; the freed princesses)
Diwali observances: Naraka Chaturdashi (pre-dawn oil bath), Lakshmi Puja; Jain and Sikh observances in the same season
